1$, or "each value appears once or twice"). That promise is a gift: **every value is also a valid index**. So a value can be sent to the slot it names, a slot can be scribbled on to remember that its value was seen, and a whole permutation can be read as a set of loops that close on themselves. This chapter turns that gift into five tools (cyclic sort, marking in place, cycle decomposition, sum and XOR bookkeeping, and permutation algebra), each of which replaces an $O(n)$-space table or an $O(n \log n)$ sort by an $O(n)$-time, $O(1)$-space pass with a short correctness proof. ::: Several earlier chapters already used this idea in passing. Frequency arrays over small values (@sec-arr-p5) spend a separate array indexed by value; hash maps (@sec-hash) pay for the same lookup when the values are large or sparse. Encoding two numbers in one cell, $\text{old} + M \cdot \text{new}$ (@eq-arr-encode in @sec-arr-inplace), is how an array keeps extra information without extra memory. Linear-time sorting introduced *value-as-index* as the zero-space end of counting sort, with sign marking and cyclic placement solving two first examples (@sec-lts-a5, @sec-lts-p2), and the pigeonhole view of a permutation with one defect (@sec-lts-p5). Partitioning treated permutations as *sequences*: the next permutation (@sec-part-perm), rank and unrank (@sec-part-rank), and rotation by juggling, which already moves elements around cycles (@sec-part-rotate-recap). This chapter treats permutations as **functions** and develops every trick fully: why it is correct, what it costs, and exactly when it breaks. It comes in two parts. **Part A** has six lessons: - **A1, the index-as-slot model.** Why "$1 \le a_i \le n$" unlocks everything, and the array as a function $i \mapsto a_i$. - **A2, cyclic sort.** Put every value at its home by swapping; at most $n$ swaps, because each swap parks a value for good. - **A3, marking in place.** Negate (or add $n$ to) the cell a value names to record "seen" without a set; restore afterwards. - **A4, permutation cycles.** Disjoint loops, the minimum number of swaps $n - c$, parity, and applying a permutation in place. - **A5, missing and duplicate values.** Sum, sum of squares, XOR and marking, and when each one is the right choice. - **A6, permutations as functions.** Composition, inverse, powers and order, all in $O(n)$ through the cycles. **Part B** spends five patterns on fourteen fully solved problems. The next chapter, @sec-mat, applies in-place marking and index arithmetic to two-dimensional arrays; the graphs volume picks up the functional-graph view for arrays that are *not* permutations (@sec-gr-p5). ## Part A — Lessons ## A1. Values in $[1, n]$: the array as its own function {#sec-idx-a1} **The idea in plain words.** If an array of length $n$ only holds numbers from $1$ to $n$, then every number can be used as an address into the same array: value $v$ "lives" at index $v - 1$. Everything in this chapter is some way of using that address. **Definition.** A length-$n$ array $a$ is *index-compatible* if $1 \le a_i \le n$ for every $i$. Then $\mathrm{home}(v) = v - 1$ is a legal index for every value, so values and positions live in the **same set** $\{0, 1, \ldots, n - 1\}$ after the shift by one. (For arrays over $0..n-1$ the shift disappears and $\mathrm{home}(v) = v$.) **The array as a function.** Any index-compatible array defines a function $f(i) = a_i - 1$ from positions to positions. Reading `a[a[i] - 1]` means "the value standing at the home of $a_i$", that is, applying $f$ twice. When every value $1..n$ appears exactly once, $a$ is a **permutation** and $f$ is a *bijection* (one-to-one and onto): it has an inverse $f^{-1}$, with $f^{-1}(j) = i$ exactly when $f(i) = j$. When some value repeats, some other value must be absent (there are $n$ slots and $n$ values), $f$ is not a bijection, and the "home" picture has a slot hit twice and a slot hit by nobody. **Why it matters.** The two pictures in @fig-idx-a1 are the whole chapter in miniature. A permutation matches values to slots perfectly, and walking its arrows gives cycles (A4, A6). A non-permutation has collisions and holes, and the tricks of A2, A3 and A5 find them. ::: {#e3af9466 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} def is_permutation(a): n = len(a) seen = [False] * n for x in a: if not (1 <= x <= n) or seen[x - 1]: return False seen[x - 1] = True return True assert is_permutation([2, 3, 1]) assert is_permutation([1]) assert not is_permutation([1, 1]) # 1 twice, so 2 is missing assert not is_permutation([2]) # 2 has no home when n = 1 assert not is_permutation([0, 2, 1]) # 0 has no home in 1..n for _ in range(200): n = random.randint(1, 8) a = [random.randint(0, n + 1) for _ in range(n)] assert is_permutation(a) == (sorted(a) == list(range(1, n + 1))) ``` ::: ::: {#fig-idx-a1} ::: {#fbcff077 .cell renderings='["light","dark"]' execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](016_index_tricks_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=569 height=264} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](016_index_tricks_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-2.png){width=569 height=264} ::: ::: Each arrow sends a value to its home slot (the bottom row shows the value each slot is the home of). Left: a permutation hits every home exactly once (green). Right: two copies of $2$ collide on one home (red) and the home of $3$ is never hit (amber). The tricks below detect, repair or exploit exactly these collisions and holes. ::: ## A2. Cyclic sort: park each value at its home {#sec-idx-a2} **The idea in plain words.** Walk through the array. Whenever the value under the cursor is not where it belongs, swap it into its home slot; the value that was sitting there comes back to the cursor and gets the same treatment. When the cursor's value is home (or cannot go home), move on. Every swap puts at least one value where it belongs for good, so the work is linear. **Algorithm.** Cursor $i$ scans left to right. Let $h = a_i - 1$ be the home of the cursor's value. $$\text{if } 0 \le h < n \text{ and } a_h \ne a_i \text{, then swap}(a_i, a_h) \text{ and stay at } i; \quad \text{else } i \leftarrow i + 1.$$ The test $a_h \ne a_i$ (rather than $a_i \ne i + 1$) is what makes the loop safe on duplicates: if the home already holds an equal value, swapping would exchange two equal values forever. The range test $0 \le h < n$ lets the loop skip values that have no home (zero, negatives, values above $n$), which is how First Missing Positive uses it. **Theorem (cyclic sort).** On any integer array the loop stops after at most $n$ swaps and $n$ advances, so it runs in $O(n)$ time with $O(1)$ extra space. Afterwards, every value $v \in 1..n$ that occurs in the array sits at index $v - 1$. On a permutation it makes exactly $n - c$ swaps, where $c$ is the number of cycles (A4), which is the minimum possible. *Proof.* A swap at cursor $i$ writes $v = a_i$ into slot $h = v - 1$, where before the swap $a_h \ne v$. After it, slot $h$ holds $v$ and is never part of a swap again: if the cursor is at $h$, its value's home is $h$ itself and the test fails; if some later cursor value has home $h$, that value is $v$ and $a_h = v$, so the test fails again. So every swap *permanently fixes a new slot*, and there are at most $n$ swaps. The cursor only moves right, so there are at most $n$ advances. When the cursor passes $i$, $a_i$ is either home, has no home, or has a home holding an equal value; so every value in $1..n$ that occurs ends at its home. On a permutation, a cycle of length $L \ge 2$ is resolved by $L - 1$ swaps, because its last swap fixes two slots at once (the value brought back to the cursor is then home too), and summing $L - 1$ over all cycles gives $n - c$. A4 proves that no method can do better. ∎ ::: {#e95ecbfb .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} def cyclic_sort(a): """Park each value v in 1..n at index v-1, in place. Returns the number of swaps.""" n = len(a) i = swaps = 0 while i < n: home = a[i] - 1 if 0 <= home < n and a[home] != a[i]: a[i], a[home] = a[home], a[i] swaps += 1 else: i += 1 return swaps def count_cycles(perm1): # cycles of a permutation of 1..n (used only to check) seen, c = set(), 0 for s in range(len(perm1)): if s not in seen: c += 1 j = s while j not in seen: seen.add(j) j = perm1[j] - 1 return c a = [4, 3, 2, 1] assert cyclic_sort(a) == 2 and a == [1, 2, 3, 4] for _ in range(300): n = random.randint(1, 12) p = random.sample(range(1, n + 1), n) a = list(p) assert cyclic_sort(a) == n - count_cycles(p) # exactly n - c swaps on a permutation assert a == list(range(1, n + 1)) b = [random.randint(-2, n + 2) for _ in range(n)] # duplicates and values without a home c = list(b) assert cyclic_sort(c) <= n assert all(c[v - 1] == v for v in set(b) if 1 <= v <= n) assert sorted(c) == sorted(b) # only a rearrangement ``` ::: ::: {#fig-idx-a2} ::: {#de879f6d .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

That bounds the search to the array's own size — and therefore lets us *store the answer set inside the array*. If the array must stay as it is, use marking (A3, restorable) or arithmetic (A5, read-only) instead. ## A3. Marking in place: negate, or add $n$ {#sec-idx-a3} **The idea in plain words.** Cyclic sort moves values. Marking leaves every value where it is and borrows a little spare room in each cell to remember something about the value whose home the cell is. The sign of a positive number is one spare bit; the "high digit" of a number stored as $\text{old} + n \cdot \text{count}$ is a whole spare counter. An index-compatible array of length $n$ has $n$ cells, one per possible value, so it can store a seen-table of $n$ entries for free. Three forms: **1. Negation (one bit per value).** For each value $v$ read from the array, look at cell $v - 1$. If it is already negative, $v$ was seen before: a duplicate. Otherwise negate it. Every read must go through $|\cdot|$, because the sign is now data, not part of the value. At the end, cells that are still positive are the homes of values that never occurred. **2. Adding $n$ (one counter per value).** Shift every value to $0..n-1$ (subtract $1$). For each position $i$, add $n$ to cell $a_i \bmod n$; the $\bmod$ recovers the original value of a cell that may already carry multiples of $n$. Afterwards cell $j$ holds $\text{orig}_j + n \cdot \text{count}(j)$ with $0 \le \text{orig}_j < n$, so $\lfloor a_j / n \rfloor$ is the number of times value $j + 1$ occurred and $a_j \bmod n$ is the original value. This is exactly the two-values-in-one-cell encoding of @eq-arr-encode, with base $M = n$. **3. Restoring.** Negation restores with $|\cdot|$, add-$n$ with $\bmod n$ (and the shift back). If the caller must get the array back unchanged, restore before returning; copying the array instead would cost the $O(n)$ space the trick was meant to save. ::: {#0bfc7230 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} def duplicates_by_sign(a): """Values in 1..n. Returns the duplicates in order of their repeat, restoring a.""" dups = [] for x in a: j = abs(x) - 1 if a[j] < 0: dups.append(j + 1) else: a[j] = -a[j] missing = [j + 1 for j in range(len(a)) if a[j] > 0] for j in range(len(a)): a[j] = abs(a[j]) return dups, missing def counts_by_adding_n(a): """Values in 1..n. Returns count[v] for v = 1..n, restoring a.""" n = len(a) for i in range(n): a[i] -= 1 # values 0..n-1: count digit starts at 0 for i in range(n): a[a[i] % n] += n # % n strips the counts already added counts = [a[j] // n for j in range(n)] for j in range(n): a[j] = a[j] % n + 1 # restore return counts arr = [3, 2, 1, 3, 4, 2] assert duplicates_by_sign(arr) == ([3, 2], [5, 6]) and arr == [3, 2, 1, 3, 4, 2] arr = [4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1] assert counts_by_adding_n(arr) == [1, 2, 2, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1] and arr == [4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1] assert counts_by_adding_n([2, 2]) == [0, 2] # the shift keeps value 2 from faking a count for _ in range(300): n = random.randint(1, 15) a = [random.randint(1, n) for _ in range(n)] b = list(a) cnt = Counter(a) assert counts_by_adding_n(b) == [cnt[v] for v in range(1, n + 1)] and b == a dups, missing = duplicates_by_sign(b) assert sorted(dups) == sorted(v for v in cnt for _ in range(cnt[v] - 1)) and b == a assert missing == [v for v in range(1, n + 1) if cnt[v] == 0] ``` ::: ::: {#fig-idx-a3} ::: {#a4914685 .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Permutation cycles, minimum swaps and parity {#sec-idx-a4} **The idea in plain words.** Take a permutation and follow it: from position $i$ go to position $p_i$, then to $p_{p_i}$, and so on. Because no two positions point to the same place, you can never walk into the middle of a loop; you must come back to where you started. So the positions split into separate loops, called **cycles**. Almost every question about a permutation (how many swaps to sort it, how often to apply it before it repeats, how to apply it in place) is answered by its cycles. **Notation.** In this lesson $p$ is 0-based: a permutation of $0..n-1$, read as the function $i \mapsto p_i$. A 1-based input is converted by subtracting one from every value. **Cycle decomposition.** Start at an unvisited $i$ and follow $i \to p_i \to p_{p_i} \to \cdots$ until you return to $i$: that is one cycle. Mark its members visited and repeat from the next unvisited position. Each position is visited once, so the decomposition costs $O(n)$. A **fixed point** ($p_i = i$) is a cycle of length $1$. In *cycle notation* the permutation $[1, 2, 0, 4, 3, 5]$ is written $(0\ 1\ 2)(3\ 4)(5)$. *Why the walk must return to $i$.* The walk visits finitely many positions, so it repeats some position. The first repeated position must be $i$: if it were some $j \ne i$, then $j$ would have two different predecessors on the walk, but in a permutation every position has exactly one preimage. ::: {#fig-idx-a4} ::: {#df77ceb2 .cell renderings='["light","dark"]' execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](016_index_tricks_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){width=520 height=334} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](016_index_tricks_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-2.png){width=520 height=334} ::: ::: The permutation $p = [3, 6, 2, 5, 7, 0, 1, 4]$ (top) drawn as arrows $i \to p_i$ (bottom). It falls apart into the cycles $(0\ 3\ 5)$, $(1\ 6)$, $(2)$ and $(4\ 7)$: $c = 4$ cycles on $n = 8$ positions. Each cell of the top row has the colour of its cycle. ::: The walk itself is the order of events that matters, so here it is as an animation: the cursor follows the arrows, colours each position with its cycle the first time it arrives, and starts a new cycle from the next uncoloured position. ::: {#fig-idx-anim-a4} ::: {#3c34b0af .cell execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Each walk starts at the leftmost uncoloured position and colours every position it passes; positions already coloured are skipped, so the total work is $n$ steps. ::: **Theorem (minimum swaps to sort).** A permutation of $n$ elements with $c$ cycles (fixed points included) needs exactly $n - c$ swaps to sort. *Proof.* Swapping the values at positions $u$ and $v$ rewires the two arrows leaving $u$ and $v$: afterwards $u \to p_v$ and $v \to p_u$. If $u$ and $v$ are on the same cycle $u \to p_u \to \cdots \to v \to p_v \to \cdots \to u$, the rewiring splits it into two cycles, $u \to p_v \to \cdots \to u$ and $v \to p_u \to \cdots \to v$. If they are on different cycles, the same rewiring splices the two loops into one. So **every swap changes $c$ by exactly $\pm 1$**. The sorted array has $n$ cycles, all fixed points, so at least $n - c$ swaps are needed. Cyclic sort (A2) uses exactly $L - 1$ swaps on each cycle of length $L$, so $n - c$ in total, which meets the bound. ∎ **Parity.** Because each swap changes $c$ by exactly one, the number of swaps in *any* sequence that sorts $p$ has the same parity as $n - c$. That parity is the **parity** (or sign) of the permutation: *even* if $n - c$ is even, *odd* otherwise. It also equals the parity of the number of inversions, since one adjacent swap changes the inversion count by exactly one. Consequences: a permutation can be sorted with exactly $m$ swaps iff $m \ge n - c$ and $m \equiv n - c \pmod 2$ (for $n \ge 2$, wasted swaps come in pairs); and puzzles that only allow moves of a fixed parity (3-cycles, the 15-puzzle) can only reach half of all arrangements. **Applying a permutation in place.** Given values $a$ and a permutation $p$ meaning "the element at position $i$ moves to position $p_i$", the result $b$ has $b_{p_i} = a_i$. With a second array this is one line. In place, carry a value around each cycle: pick up $a_i$, drop it at $p_i$ while picking up what was there, continue to $p_{p_i}$, and stop when you are back at $i$. To know which cycles are done without a visited array, mark $p$ itself (A3): replace a visited $p_j$ by its bitwise complement $\lnot p_j = -p_j - 1$, which is negative even when $p_j = 0$, and complement again at the end. ::: {#3fa02283 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} def cycles_of(p): n = len(p) seen = [False] * n out = [] for s in range(n): if not seen[s]: cyc, j = [], s while not seen[j]: seen[j] = True cyc.append(j) j = p[j] out.append(cyc) return out def min_swaps(p): return len(p) - len(cycles_of(p)) def inversions(p): return sum(1 for i in range(len(p)) for j in range(i + 1, len(p)) if p[i] > p[j]) def apply_in_place(a, p): """Move a[i] to position p[i] for every i, in place; Missing and duplicate numbers: sum, XOR, marking {#sec-idx-a5} **The idea in plain words.** If you know what the array *should* contain (all of $1..n$, say), compare a summary of what it *does* contain with a summary of what it should. A sum or an XOR of everything cancels all the values that are present and leaves only the difference. One unknown needs one equation; a missing value *and* a duplicate need two. For an array that should be $1..n$: - **Sum, one gap.** If the array holds $n - 1$ distinct values of $1..n$, the missing one is $\frac{n(n+1)}{2} - \sum a_i$. Pick any set bit of $x$, for example the lowest, $x \mathbin{\&} {-x}$. It splits all numbers (the range and the array) into two groups; $m$ and $d$ land in different groups, and every other value cancels within its own group. XOR each group separately to get $\{m, d\}$, and one more pass over the array tells which one is the duplicate. Overflow-free, read-only. - **Marking.** A3's negation finds both in one pass: the duplicate when a cell is already negative, the missing value as the cell still positive. Permutations as functions: compose, invert, iterate {#sec-idx-a6} **The idea in plain words.** A permutation is a rule "position $i$ goes to position $p_i$". Rules can be done one after another (composition), undone (inverse), and repeated $k$ times (powers). Each of these is one short loop over the array, and repeating a rule many times is cheap once you know its cycles: on a cycle of length $L$, doing the rule $L$ times is the same as doing nothing. Throughout, $p$ and $q$ are 0-based permutations of $0..n-1$. - **Composition.** $(p \circ q)(i) = p(q(i))$: first $q$, then $p$. As arrays, $r_i = p[q_i]$, a *gather* (read from the position the data names). Composition is associative but not commutative: $p \circ q \ne q \circ p$ in general. LC 1920 computes $p \circ p$, in place with the encoding of @eq-arr-encode (@sec-arr-p4-b). - **Inverse.** $p^{-1}$ undoes $p$: $p^{-1}(p(i)) = i$. As arrays, $s[p_i] = i$, a *scatter* (write to the position the data names), $O(n)$. The inverse of a composition reverses the order: $(p \circ q)^{-1} = q^{-1} \circ p^{-1}$, like taking off socks and shoes. - **Powers.** $p^k$ is $p$ applied $k$ times. Repeated composition costs $O(nk)$ (or $O(n \log k)$ by repeated squaring), but the cycles give $O(n)$ for any $k$: on a cycle $(c_0\ c_1\ \cdots\ c_{L-1})$, $p^k(c_t) = c_{(t + k) \bmod L}$. - **Order.** The smallest $k \ge 1$ with $p^k = \mathrm{id}$ is $\operatorname{lcm}$ of the cycle lengths: each cycle of length $L$ returns exactly at the multiples of $L$, and all of them return together at the common multiples. For the smallest result, walk left to right and also overwrite a *first* copy of $v$ when a smaller gap is waiting and another copy of $v$ is still to come. ::: ::: {.p-approach} 1. **Try every permutation.** For tiny $n$, compare $a$ with every permutation, count the positions that differ, and keep the smallest $(q, \text{permutation})$ pair. $O(n! \cdot n)$: the definition, and the oracle for the stress test. 2. **Count the gaps.** Build `freq[v]`. Let `missing` be the values with `freq[v] = 0`. Each move can fill at most one gap, so $q \ge |\text{missing}|$; and overwriting one spare copy per gap achieves it, because $\sum_v (\text{freq}[v] - 1)^{+} = |\text{missing}|$ (both sides equal $n$ minus the number of distinct values). So $q = |\text{missing}|$, and the cells to change are *exactly* the spare copies. 3. **Keep the first copy.** Walk left to right; keep the first copy of each value and overwrite every later copy with the next missing value, in increasing order. This uses $q$ moves and yields a permutation, but not the smallest one: on $[3, 2, 2, 3]$ it gives $[3, 2, 1, 4]$, while $[1, 2, 4, 3]$ is smaller. 4. **Lex-min greedy.** Track `cnt[v]`, the copies of $v$ at or after the current cell, and `used[v]`, whether a copy of $v$ has been kept. At a cell holding $v$ (after decrementing `cnt[v]`): if `used[v]`, the cell is a spare, so write the smallest waiting missing value. Otherwise, if that missing value $m$ is smaller than $v$ **and** `cnt[v]` $\ge 1$ (another $v$ is still to come and can be kept later), write $m$. Otherwise keep $v$ and set `used[v]`. **Why the greedy is optimal.** Every answer with $q$ moves rewrites exactly the spare copies, one per value with `freq[v] > 1` kept. So the only freedom is *which* copy of each repeated value survives, and which gap goes where. Missing values must be written in increasing order of position (a swap of two written values that are out of order gives a smaller result). At the first cell, keeping $v$ when a smaller $m$ waits and $v$ recurs is never better: overwriting with $m$ makes the prefix smaller, and $v$ can still be kept at a later copy. Keeping $v$ when $m > v$ is better than writing $m$. When $v$ does not recur and has not been kept, this is its last copy, and overwriting it would lose $v$. Each decision is forced, so the result is the smallest. **Worked trace (lex-min).** $[3, 2, 2, 3]$, `missing = [1, 4]`. Cell $0$ holds $3$: $1 < 3$ waits and another $3$ comes later, so write $1$. Splitting only refines the partition of indices into cycles: two indices that start on different cycles can never end on the same one. So if $k$ and $k + 1$ share a cycle, split everything else off and keep them together, $n - 1 - c$ swaps. A length-4 array with MEX $3$ contains $0, 1, 2$ and one more value $y \ne 3$; its XOR is $3 \oplus y$, which is $0$ only for $y = 3$. A length-5 witness: $[0, 1, 2, 4, 7]$, with XOR $3 \oplus 4 \oplus 7 = 0$ and no $3$ (@sec-idx-p4-mexor). ::: **12. [M] An array of length $n$ holds $1..n$ with one value doubled and one missing, $[1, 2, 2, 4]$. Recover both with the XOR split, showing the groups.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"} XOR of $1..4$ and the array: $(1 \oplus 2 \oplus 3 \oplus 4) \oplus (1 \oplus 2 \oplus 2 \oplus 4) = 4 \oplus 5 = 1 = m \oplus d$. Lowest set bit: $1$. Odd group: range $\{1, 3\}$ and array $\{1\}$, XOR $= 3$. Even group: range $\{2, 4\}$ and array $\{2, 2, 4\}$, XOR $= 2$. So $\{m, d\} = \{3, 2\}$; $2$ occurs in the array, so $d = 2$ and $m = 3$ (@sec-idx-a5). ::: **13. [M] Show that rotating an array of length $n$ left by $k$ has exactly $\gcd(n, k)$ cycles, each of length $n / \gcd(n, k)$.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"} On positions the rotation is $i \mapsto (i - k) \bmod n$, so the cycle of $i$ is $\{i - tk \bmod n : t \ge 0\}$. Its length is the smallest $t \ge 1$ with $tk \equiv 0 \pmod n$, which is $n / \gcd(n, k)$, the same for every $i$. All cycles having that length, there are $n / (n / \gcd(n, k)) = \gcd(n, k)$ of them. Positions $i$ and $j$ share a cycle iff $i \equiv j \pmod{\gcd(n, k)}$, so the residues $0, \ldots, \gcd(n, k) - 1$ are one representative each: the juggling rotation starts one walk from each (@sec-idx-a4, @sec-part-rotate-recap). ::: **14. [M] A permutation can be sorted with $3$ swaps. Can it be sorted with exactly $4$? With exactly $5$?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"} If $3$ swaps suffice, then $n - c \le 3$ and $n - c \equiv 3 \pmod 2$, so $n - c \in \{1, 3\}$, odd. Every sorting sequence has the parity of $n - c$, so exactly $4$ is impossible. Exactly $5$ is possible: sort in $n - c$ swaps, then swap one pair twice to burn the remaining even number (@sec-idx-a4). ::: **15. [M] Characterise the permutations that equal their own inverse, and count them for $n = 4$.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"} $p = p^{-1}$ iff $p \circ p = \mathrm{id}$ iff every cycle has length $1$ or $2$: a cycle of length $L$ returns after two steps only if $L \mid 2$. For $n = 4$: the identity ($1$), one transposition ($\binom{4}{2} = 6$), two disjoint transpositions ($3$): $10$ in total (@sec-idx-a6). ::: **16. [M] Prove that $(p \circ q)^{-1} = q^{-1} \circ p^{-1}$ and say what it means for undoing two shuffles.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"} $(q^{-1} \circ p^{-1}) \circ (p \circ q) = q^{-1} \circ (p^{-1} \circ p) \circ q = q^{-1} \circ q = \mathrm{id}$ by associativity, and the inverse is unique. To undo "first $q$, then $p$", undo $p$ first and then $q$: the last shuffle applied is the first one undone (@sec-idx-a6). ::: **17. [H] Prove that one swap changes the number of cycles of a permutation by exactly $\pm 1$.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"} Swapping the values at positions $u \ne v$ changes only the two arrows leaving $u$ and $v$: $u \to p_v$ and $v \to p_u$. Every other cycle is untouched. Same cycle: it reads $u \to p_u \to \cdots \to v \to p_v \to \cdots \to u$; after rewiring, $u \to p_v \to \cdots \to u$ and $v \to p_u \to \cdots \to v$ are two separate loops, $+1$. Different cycles $u \to p_u \to \cdots \to u$ and $v \to p_v \to \cdots \to v$: after rewiring, $u \to p_v \to \cdots \to v \to p_u \to \cdots \to u$ is one loop, $-1$. Hence the minimum $n - c$ of @sec-idx-a4. ::: **18. [H] Prove that the CF 864D greedy (@sec-idx-p1-makeperm) returns the lexicographically smallest permutation among those with $q$ changes.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"} With exactly $q$ changes, every value that occurs keeps exactly one of its copies and every missing value is written once, so a solution is fixed by choosing one surviving copy per occurring value and assigning missing values to the remaining cells. Among assignments, increasing order of the missing values from left to right is smallest (swapping two out-of-order written values makes the earlier position smaller). Now compare the greedy with an optimal answer $r^*$ at the first cell $i$ where they differ; cell $i$ holds $v$. If the greedy writes $m < v$ there, then $v$ recurs later and $m$ is the smallest unwritten missing value; $r^*$ keeps $v$ at $i$ (writing any other missing value would be larger than $m$), so moving $v$'s survivor to a later copy of $v$ and writing $m$ at $i$ is valid and smaller, contradicting optimality. If the greedy keeps $v$, then either $v$ does not recur (overwriting it would lose $v$) or the smallest missing value exceeds $v$ (overwriting makes cell $i$ larger); either way $r^*$ cannot be smaller at $i$. If $v$ is already kept, both must overwrite with the same smallest missing value. So no first difference exists. ::: **19. [H] Invert a permutation of $0..n-1$ in place, with $O(1)$ extra memory and $O(n)$ time.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"} Walk each cycle once and reverse its arrows, marking finished positions with the complement trick of @sec-idx-a4. For a start $s$ with $p_s \ge 0$: keep `prev = s`, `j = p[s]`; while $j \ne s$, read `nxt = p[j]`, write `p[j] = ~prev` (the inverse sends $j$ back to its predecessor, marked), set `prev = j`, `j = nxt`; finally `p[s] = ~prev`. After all cycles, complement every entry. Each position is written once and read twice: $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra. On $[1, 2, 0]$: the cycle $0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 0$ becomes $p_1 = 0$, $p_2 = 1$, $p_0 = 2$, so $p^{-1} = [2, 0, 1]$. Knuth's TAOCP §1.3.3 gives a variant without the complement marks. ::: **20. [H] An array of $n + 1$ integers from $1..n$ is read-only, and one value may repeat many times. Why do sums fail, and what replaces them?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"} If the repeated value $d$ occurs $r$ times, the sum is $\frac{n(n+1)}{2} - (\text{missing values}) + (r - 1)d$, with an unknown number of unknown missing values: one equation cannot recover $d$. Read the array as the function $i \mapsto a_i$ on indices $0..n$. Index $0$ has no preimage (values are at least $1$), so the walk from $0$ enters a cycle after a tail, and the cycle's entry point has two preimages, one on the tail and one on the cycle: that entry is the repeated value. Floyd's tortoise and hare finds it in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space without writing. This is LC 287, solved in @sec-gr-p5-duplicate. ::: ## Interview questions **1. Why is cyclic sort $O(n)$ when it has a `while` loop that does not always advance?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Count events, not loop shapes. Each iteration either advances the cursor (at most $n$ times) or swaps, and every swap writes a value into its home slot, after which that slot is never swapped again. So there are at most $n$ swaps and at most $2n$ iterations in total (@sec-idx-a2). ::: **2. When would you use cyclic sort rather than a hash set or a counting array on $1..n$ data?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} When $O(1)$ extra space is required and the array may be rearranged. A counting array is simpler when $O(n)$ memory is fine; a hash set when values are not in a small known range; marking (@sec-idx-a3) when the input order must survive; arithmetic (@sec-idx-a5) when the array is read-only. ::: **3. Find all duplicates in an array of $n$ values from $1..n$ in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space. What precondition does your method need, and how do you undo the damage?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Negation marking: for each $x$, look at cell $|x| - 1$; if it is negative, $|x|$ is a duplicate, else negate it. It needs values in $1..n$ and all positive (zero has no sign to flip). Read every value through `abs`, and restore with a final `abs` pass. Cyclic sort also works and reports the values left in misfit slots, but it rearranges the array (@sec-idx-p1-dups). ::: **4. State and prove the minimum number of swaps to sort a permutation.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} $n - c$, with $c$ the number of cycles including fixed points. A swap rewires two arrows, so it splits one cycle or merges two: $c$ changes by exactly one. Sorted means $n$ cycles, so at least $n - c$ swaps; cyclic sort uses $L - 1$ swaps per cycle of length $L$, which is $n - c$ in total (@sec-idx-a4). ::: **5. What is the minimum number of *adjacent* swaps to sort a permutation, and why is it different?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} The number of inversions. An adjacent swap changes the inversion count by exactly one, and while the array is unsorted some adjacent pair is inverted, so swapping it reduces the count by one (bubble sort). Arbitrary swaps can fix far-apart elements at once, which is why $n - c$ can be much smaller. Both counts have the same parity (@sec-idx-a4). ::: **6. Given a permutation and $K$ up to $10^{18}$, output the permutation applied $K$ times.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Decompose into cycles once, $O(n)$. On a cycle $c_0 \ldots c_{L-1}$, the element at offset $t$ goes to offset $(t + K) \bmod L$. Each position costs $O(1)$, so $O(n)$ in total, with no dependence on $K$. Repeated squaring of the permutation would cost $O(n \log K)$; simulation is hopeless (@sec-idx-a6). ::: **7. When does a permutation first return to the identity under repeated application, and why can the answer be huge?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} At the lcm of its cycle lengths: each cycle of length $L$ is home exactly at multiples of $L$. Cycle lengths can be pairwise coprime ($2 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 11 = 28$ elements give order $2310$), so the order grows much faster than $n$; compute it with 64-bit lcm, never by simulation (@sec-idx-a6, @sec-idx-p5-shift). ::: **8. One number is missing and one is doubled in $1..n$. Compare sum, XOR and marking when the array is read-only and $n$ is large.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Read-only rules out marking. A single sum gives $m - d$ and a single XOR gives $m \oplus d$: one equation each, two unknowns. Add the sum of squares ($m^2 - d^2$, so $m + d = S_2 / S_1$), watching for overflow of $\sum a_i^2$; or split the XOR by a set bit of $m \oplus d$, which never overflows, and use one more pass to tell $m$ from $d$ (@sec-idx-a5). ::: **9. Define the MEX. How do you compute the MEX of $n$ integers in $O(n)$, and why is it at most $n$?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} The smallest non-negative integer not present. Among the $n + 1$ candidates $0..n$, at most $n$ can be present, so some value $\le n$ is missing. Mark the values in $0..n$ in a boolean table (ignore larger ones) and scan for the first unmarked entry; with a writable array of non-negative values, the marking can be done in place (@sec-idx-a3, @sec-idx-p2-mex). ::: **10. Find a duplicate among $n + 1$ integers from $1..n$ without modifying the array and in $O(1)$ extra space.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Read the array as the function $i \mapsto a_i$ on indices $0..n$. There are $n + 1$ indices and only $n$ values, so some value has two preimages (pigeonhole), and the walk from index $0$ ends in a cycle whose entry point is that value. Floyd's tortoise and hare finds the entry in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space. Solved in @sec-gr-p5-duplicate. ::: **11. What exactly does add-$n$ marking store, and why can you recover both the count and the original value?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} After shifting to $0..n-1$, cell $j$ ends as $\text{orig}_j + n \cdot \text{count}_j$ with $0 \le \text{orig}_j < n$. Division by $n$ with remainder is unique, so `a[j] // n` is the count and `a[j] % n` is the original. During the pass, every index must be computed as `a[i] % n`, because the cell being read may already carry counts (@sec-idx-a3, @eq-arr-encode). ::: **12. How do you apply a permutation to an array in place?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Follow each cycle once, carrying one value: pick up $a_s$, drop it at $p_s$ while picking up what was there, and continue until you are back at $s$. To skip finished cycles without a visited array, mark $p_j$ when visiting $j$ (by complementing it, which works even for the value $0$) and restore $p$ at the end. $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra (@sec-idx-a4). ::: **13. Can every permutation be sorted with exactly $m$ swaps for any large $m$?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} No: only for $m \ge n - c$ with $m \equiv n - c \pmod 2$ (and $n \ge 2$). Each swap changes the number of cycles by exactly one, so the parity of the swap count is fixed by the permutation. Extra swaps can only be wasted in pairs (@sec-idx-a4). ::: **14. Your function marks the input in place and restores it before returning. Is it really "read-only"?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Only from the caller's sequential view. During the call the array is visibly modified, so another thread or an alias holding a reference sees negative values; and an exception mid-pass leaves it corrupted. Say so in an interview: in-place marking trades memory for atomicity, and a truly read-only input calls for the arithmetic of @sec-idx-a5 or Floyd's walk (@sec-idx-a3). ::: **15. For CF 864D, why is the number of changes fixed before you decide which copies to overwrite?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Each value that occurs $c > 1$ times has $c - 1$ spare copies, and each missing value is one gap. Both totals equal $n$ minus the number of distinct values, so $q = $ number of gaps is forced by the frequency table alone. What depends on the order is *which* copies to overwrite, and that only decides the lexicographic order of the result (@sec-idx-p1-makeperm). ::: **16. Why is the inverse of a permutation a scatter and composition a gather?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Composition $r_i = p[q_i]$ *reads* from the position named by the data, which is a gather. The inverse needs, for each value $v$, the position holding it; knowing only $p$, the natural loop visits each position $i$ and *writes* $i$ to the position $p_i$, which is a scatter. Writing the inverse as a gather would need a search per value, $O(n^2)$ (@sec-idx-a6, @sec-idx-p5-presents). ::: ## Summary ::: {.callout-important title="Templates to remember"} - **Cyclic sort:** `while i < n: h = a[i]-1; if 0 <= h < n and a[h] != a[i]: swap(a[i], a[h]) else: i += 1`. At most $n$ swaps; exactly $n - c$ on a permutation (@sec-idx-a2, @sec-idx-p1). - **Marking:** negate cell $|x| - 1$ for a seen bit, read with `abs`; add $n$ to cell $a_i \bmod n$ for a count, read `// n` and `% n`; restore afterwards (@sec-idx-a3, @sec-idx-p2). - **Cycles:** one walk per cycle, $O(n)$. Minimum swaps $n - c$; parity of $n - c$ is the parity of any sorting sequence; apply a permutation in place by carrying a value round each cycle (@sec-idx-a4, @sec-idx-p3). - **Missing values by arithmetic:** $\frac{n(n+1)}{2} - \sum a_i$ (64-bit) or XOR of the range and the array; two unknowns need sum of squares or the XOR split; $f(t) = 0 \oplus \cdots \oplus t = [t, 1, t+1, 0][t \bmod 4]$ (@sec-idx-a5, @sec-idx-p4). - **Permutation algebra:** inverse `q[p[i]] = i`; composition `r[i] = p[q[i]]`; power along cycles with $(t + k) \bmod L$; order $=$ lcm of cycle lengths (@sec-idx-a6, @sec-idx-p5). ::: - Every trick here is one observation: **values in $1..n$ are also indices in $0..n-1$**, so the array can index itself, remember for itself and point at itself (@sec-idx-a1). - Cyclic sort is counting sort performed inside its own output array; each swap fixes a slot for good, which is both the linear-time proof and the $n - c$ swap count (@sec-idx-a2). - Marking stores one bit (sign) or one counter (multiple of $n$) per value inside the cells; its preconditions are the price list: positive values, `abs` reads, `% n` reads, 64-bit cells, a restore pass (@sec-idx-a3). - A permutation is a set of independent loops. Swaps split or merge loops one at a time, which gives the minimum swap count, the parity, and the impossibility arguments (@sec-idx-a4, @sec-idx-p3). - Sums and XORs compare the array with what it should be without touching it; the number of equations must match the number of unknowns (@sec-idx-a5, @sec-idx-p4). - Composition, inverse and powers are $O(n)$ loops; repeated application is periodic per cycle, so large exponents reduce modulo cycle lengths and return times are lcms (@sec-idx-a6, @sec-idx-p5). - When the arrows $i \to a_i$ are not a bijection, walks become $\rho$-shaped and the tools move to the graphs volume (@sec-gr-p5). ## Practice ladder Ordered by concept: cyclic sort, marking, cycles, arithmetic, permutation algebra.
